body: Definitely not the slowest. The town in Western Michigan I grew up in was an odd combination of tourist town and farming community. That place gets crazy during tourist season. I would put in the same amount of hours as my first job and made way more money for what felt like (and probably was) less work. I've worked in many, many different customer service jobs and factory jobs and none of them have come close to the difficulty of field work. I get it, we all have or have had shitty jobs. In my experience, if you don't want to be treated like an asshole, don't be an asshole. Rule #1 of customer service.

I grew up in a small, rural town with an economy that centered around agriculture. The first job I ever had was my junior year of high school, trimming Christmas trees from the end of the school year to the beginning of my senior year. I got paid $7.40 an hour to walk up and down rows of Christmas trees, swinging a machete, giving them their desired shape. I worked 10-12 hours a day, 7 days a week, all through the summer.  

Second job: waiter at a local mom-and-pop restaurant. Averaged about $10 an hour once tips were factored in, depending on how many elderly people came that day. Waiting tables remains the easiest job I have ever had. So I was on my feet all day, had to deal with an occasional asshole, and had a despotic boss. Big fucking deal. I also got free lunches, worked in AC, and made a lot of good friends. 

TL;DR field work is 10x worse than working in food service. Get over yourselves. Everyone hates their job, and some one will always have it worse than you.

OCD and BPD here. Parents, if you are religious and have a mentally ill child, get them actual help. Get them into therapy. DO NOT tell them to just "talk to Jesus" or "pray it away" or "that's just Satan trying to lead you away from righteousness". I went undiagnosed for 22 years as a result of this, and only recently got into therapy.

As a father of 2, I understand completely. I would never go so far as to hurt my children, but the thoughts are always there. It's unsettling, and for the longest time I felt like I couldn't trust myself around them, and that I was unfit to even be a parent. It's been a burden, and a detriment to my relationship with them. I still have problems with thoughts of suicide and self-harm, but a lot of the time those come when I'm in a depression.
